issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states in the Measures section that only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. However, in the Data Screening section, it states that measures of problematic use will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This contradiction drastically affects the analytic plan, sample sizes, and potential for zero-inflation in the regression models.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. [vs] That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.
issues.location: Method (Measures vs Data Screening and Inclusion Criteria)

issues.description: The analytic plan states the equivalence region is based on a SESOI of δ = .27. Two paragraphs later, it states the SESOI is set to β = .11, and that setting the region to δ = |.11| is an extremely conservative decision. It is entirely unclear what the primary equivalence bound is for the well-powered analyses.
issues.quote: with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. [vs] we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11...)

issues.subcategory: Incorrect test logic for effect comparison
issues.description: To test if the substance use interaction is smaller than the pornography interaction when underpowered, the authors propose an equivalence test using the lower bound of the pornography effect (β = .27) as the equivalence region [-0.27, 0.27]. Finding an effect within this region only proves the effect is between -.27 and .27; it does not statistically test whether the substance effect is significantly smaller than the pornography effect. Furthermore, an equivalence bound of β = .27 is excessively wide for an interaction term, guaranteeing a conclusion of 'equivalence' for almost any realistic effect.
issues.quote: we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography (β = .27...)

issues.description: The text states the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) uses a 4-point scale of 0 to 3. However, the supplemental materials table lists the response anchors as Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), and Almost Always (5). Using these incorrect, non-linear numerical anchors will severely distort the scoring and validity of the PGSI.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.description: The text describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using a 'three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)'. However, the supplemental materials table for the BPS lists the anchors as 'Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4)'. Summing these incorrect values will alter the scale's maximum score and invalidate comparisons to established norms.
issues.quote: three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often) [vs] Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.description: The authors propose averaging the 5 problematic use items of the NIDA-ASSIST. The ASSIST has a validated scoring algorithm based on weighted sum scores to determine clinical risk levels. Whether they average raw scores (which is mathematically flawed due to mixing 0-5 and 0,3,6 scales) or average standardized item scores, they are deviating from the validated scoring method, which undermines the clinical relevance and validity of the measure.
issues.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST.

issues.description: The study combines a 2,500 nationally representative sample with a 1,500 oversample of sports bettors. Analyzing this combined sample of 4,000 without applying survey weights will result in a highly skewed, non-representative sample (overrepresenting males, younger people, and gamblers). This violates the claim of testing these effects in a representative sample.
issues.quote: This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: The authors aim to compare the effect of moral incongruence across different behaviors to show it is unique to pornography. However, they use different dependent variables for the primary analyses (BPS for porn, PGSI for gambling, ASSIST for substances). Differences in the interaction effect sizes could be driven by the psychometric properties (reliability, variance, sensitivity) of the different scales rather than true theoretical differences in the constructs.
issues.quote: with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.description: The manuscript provides contradictory instructions on how the interaction terms will be calculated. In one paragraph, it states predictors and moderators will be centered before calculating the interaction. In the next paragraph, it states variables will be entered in their raw form and their product computed. This affects the interpretation of main effects in the regression model.
issues.quote: focal predictors... and moderators... will be centered and their interaction term calculated. [vs] key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: Ambiguity in models to be tested
issues.description: The authors state they are including modified NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography and gambling to 'allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors'. However, the analytic plan states they will conduct 8 moderation analyses, specifically mentioning the use of the BPS and PGSI for porn and gambling. It is entirely unclear if the parallel ASSIST models for porn and gambling will be run as primary tests, secondary tests, or at all.
issues.quote: These will be included to allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors and substances... In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses... with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom for robustness
issues.description: The authors state that if regression assumptions are violated, they will conduct supplemental analyses. If the results 'remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same)', they will present the OLS results. This introduces analytic flexibility. It is not specified which model becomes the primary inference if the results are not robust.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results

issues.description: The authors state they 'anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' because of YouGov's quality control. This is an unrealistic assumption for a survey of 4,000 people on sensitive topics (pornography, illicit drugs). There is no stated plan for how missing data (e.g., item non-response) will be handled (e.g., FIML, multiple imputation, listwise deletion) if it does occur.
issues.quote: we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.description: Hypotheses 2a and 3a specifically predict effects 'among gamblers' and 'among substance users'. However, if the authors follow their data screening plan to 'administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample' and include them in the regression, they will be testing the effect among the entire population (including non-users), not just among users.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems

issues.subcategory: Unclear evaluation of main effects in moderation models
issues.description: Hypotheses 1a, 2a, and 3a predict significant 'direct effects' of moral disapproval while controlling for covariates. It is not specified whether these main effects will be tested in a separate main-effects-only regression model or interpreted from the moderation model. If interpreted from the moderation model, the main effect represents the effect of disapproval at a specific level of frequency (zero if uncentered, mean if centered), which changes the interpretation entirely.
issues.quote: We expect to find that the simple, direct effect of moral disapproval of pornography on self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be significant and positive, even when use frequency, religiousness, gender, and age are included as covariates in a regression model.

issues.description: The text states there are 8 target behaviors/variables of interest and that 8 moderation analyses will be conducted. However, only 7 behaviors are listed in the text and tables (pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs). It is unclear what the 8th outcome is.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.description: The text states the frequency scale for pornography and gambling ranges from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day), and for ASSIST it ranges from 0 to 5. However, the supplemental tables show all frequency measures using a 0 to 5 scale.
issues.quote: scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day) [vs] scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)

issues.description: The authors plan to run at least 7 moderation analyses (each testing multiple main effects and an interaction) but do not mention any correction for family-wise error rate or false discovery rate for these primary regression models, despite mentioning Holm adjustments for bivariate correlations.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency

issues.subcategory: Inflated Type I error in equivalence testing
issues.description: The authors propose using the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test. Methodological literature notes that the Anderson-Hauck test can be overly liberal and inflate Type I error rates (falsely concluding equivalence) under certain conditions compared to the standard TOST procedure. This biases the results toward confirming their hypotheses of null effects.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015)

issues.subcategory: Conflation of moral distress and moral incongruence
issues.description: The authors justify the study based on the ICD-11 caveat that 'moral distress' is not sufficient for a CSBD diagnosis. However, they operationalize their test using 'moral incongruence' (the interaction of disapproval and frequency). Finding that the interaction is unique to pornography does not directly test or support the ICD-11 caveat, which pertains to the main effect of moral distress/disapproval.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.description: Despite acknowledging the cross-sectional nature of the data in the limitations, the authors repeatedly use causal language such as 'predicts', 'influences', and 'driving' when describing the relationships between moral disapproval, frequency, and self-reported addiction.
issues.quote: whether moral incongruence... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.description: The authors state gender will be coded as a binary variable (1 = male, 0 = not-male). It is unclear how non-binary or transgender participants will be handled. Grouping women and non-binary individuals into a 'not-male' category may obscure important differences.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.description: The authors combine smoked tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and e-cigarettes/vapes into a single item for both frequency and moral disapproval. Moral attitudes and use patterns likely differ significantly across these distinct products, meaning a single combined item may lack validity and obscure specific relationships.
issues.quote: we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.description: The analytic plan states that moderation analyses will be conducted using the `lm` function in R. However, a later paragraph states that 'Interactions will be tested using this program [the Interactive Shiny application]'. It is unclear which software/method is the primary analytic tool for hypothesis testing versus visualization.
issues.quote: we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R [vs] Interactions will be tested using this program [Interactive Shiny application]
